title: Meet your Linux terminal
intro: The terminal is your text window; Bash interprets your instructions. Programs ask the kernel for resources, like staff asking hospital logistics for equipment. Keep this handbook open and execute commands in the second tab.
task: In your Codespace terminal, ask for the kernel name with uname. Paste its output. If it is Darwin or Windows, switch to the Codespace Linux terminal.
question: Which component interprets your command line?
why: Bash parses the command and launches programs. The terminal displays input and output; the kernel manages system resources.

title: Locate the evidence
intro: Before inspecting a server, establish your identity and location. pwd prints your current directory; ls lists entries, and a path argument selects another directory. In ls -la data, -l adds details, -a includes hidden names, and data is the directory to inspect.
task: List data/logs instead. Enter all three log filenames; order and spacing do not matter.
question: Which command prints your current directory?
why: pwd prints location; whoami names the user; uname identifies the kernel.

title: Follow a different branch
intro: Directories form a tree, like wards branching from a hospital entrance. cd changes directory, pwd confirms your location, and .. means the parent directory. Relative paths start where you stand; absolute paths begin at /. Start this example at the repository root and return with cd ../.. afterwards.
task: Return to the repository root, then enter data/logs. Run pwd and paste its output. Return to the root afterwards.
question: From data/logs, which path reaches data/config?
why: .. reaches data; ../config then enters its config child.

title: Protect a configuration snapshot
intro: A working copy protects original evidence, like a photocopy of a clinical form. mkdir -p creates folders, cp copies source to destination, and cat prints file contents. Run the example from the repository root to prepare your work folders. For your transfer, cmp -s compares two files silently; echo $? prints 0 when they match.
command:
mkdir -p work/scratch work/reports work/logs
cp data/logs/platform.log work/logs/platform.log
cp data/config/platform.conf work/scratch/example.conf
cat work/scratch/example.conf
task: Copy data/config/platform.conf.backup to work/scratch/review.conf. Run cmp -s data/config/platform.conf.backup work/scratch/review.conf; echo $? and enter the result. Keep review.conf for the final file check.
question: Which action keeps its source?
why: cp creates a second copy. mv relocates the original entry; rm removes it.

title: Investigate a new upload snapshot
intro: A log is a timeline of observations, like a delivery tracking history. grep selects lines containing a pattern; -c counts matching lines instead of printing them. Matching is case-sensitive, and a failed recorded attempt alone does not establish clinical harm.
task: Count ERROR records in data/upload_small.log and print only the count. Run any correct Linux command or pipeline in the command field below.
question: Four ERROR records establish…
why: Events can concern the same device repeatedly. Clinical impact needs additional evidence.

title: Scale up and save evidence
intro: A pipe | is a conveyor belt: it sends one command’s output into the next. wc -l counts lines, while > saves output to a file, replacing any existing contents; >> appends instead. Recall grep from the previous step, then apply it to the larger dataset. Work from the repository root and save only under work/.
task: Create work/reports if needed. Save only ERROR records from data/logs/upload.log as work/reports/upload-errors.txt. Count the saved lines and paste the result. Keep the file for the final check.
question: What does > do to an existing destination?
why: > replaces contents before the program runs. >> appends; | connects standard output to standard input.

title: Verify your investigation
intro: Combine navigation, safe copies, searching and saved evidence. Complete the incident mission above and the transfer tasks from chapters 4 and 6. The checker reads your files without running any pasted commands.
task: Mini-project: analyse work/logs/platform.log. Count all records, ERRORs and WARNs; save ERRORs to work/reports/errors.txt and connection_refused records to work/reports/storage-errors.txt. Inspect all band-03 events and its final observation. Write work/reports/incident.txt (100–150 words) with the time window, counts, one exact evidence line, reproducible commands, one limitation and a next investigation. Include the device name band-03. Keep the transfer files from chapters 4 and 6. Run python3 scripts/check_work.py and paste the complete JSON below. A peer should review the interpretation.
question: A final accepted upload proves…
options: that one later attempt was accepted
why: Keep the conclusion within the observation: one later recorded success is limited evidence.
